title: Markup vs Margin: Stop Underpricing Your Work

scenes.narration: You added 20 percent to your costs. You called it margin. You actually got 16.7 percent. And that gap repeats on every single job.
lines: That gap costs you thousands every year.

scenes.narration: Confusing markup with margin is quietly underpricing your work. Across materials, labor, subcontractors, and a whole year, it can be the difference between paying yourself properly and wondering where the money went.
lines: Markup is added to cost. Margin is what you keep.
Using them interchangeably is costing you.

scenes.narration: Here is the simple truth. Buy materials for one thousand dollars. Add twenty percent markup. You charge twelve hundred dollars. That is two hundred dollars profit — which is only a sixteen point seven percent margin. To get a real twenty percent margin, you needed to charge twelve fifty. A twenty five percent markup equals a twenty percent margin. They are not the same number.

Let us look at a real panel upgrade. Your direct costs total two thousand four hundred dollars. You want a twenty percent margin. The correct price is three thousand dollars — leaving six hundred dollars profit. Now apply a twenty percent markup instead. You quote twenty eight eighty. Your profit drops to four hundred eighty. Your margin falls to sixteen point seven percent. You left one hundred twenty dollars on the table before the job even started.
lines: You just lost $120. On one job.

scenes.narration: Now a bathroom renovation. Five thousand dollars in direct costs, plus four hundred in overhead for insurance, your vehicle, phone, software, and quoting time. Your real cost is five thousand four hundred dollars. A twenty percent markup on every line gives you a six thousand dollar quote. After costs and overhead, your profit is only six hundred dollars. That is a ten percent margin. Ten percent. To get twenty percent, you needed to charge six thousand seven hundred fifty. You left seven hundred fifty dollars behind on a single job.

Three places contractors lose the most money. One: marking up materials but guessing on everything else. Two: forgetting overhead. Van payments, insurance, tools, software — they do not show up on a receipt, but they must show up in your price. Three: passing along subcontractor invoices at cost. You carried the scheduling risk and you are responsible for the result. Include the sub in your total cost, then apply your target margin.
lines: 3. Passing subs at cost with zero margin

scenes.narration: The fix is simple. Before every estimate, write down four numbers: every direct cost, your overhead allocation, your target margin, and the resulting price. Then check those same numbers after the job. Your estimate might have been right while the job ran long. Either way, you will know instead of guessing.
lines: The Fix: 4 Numbers Before Every Job
Check them again when the job is done.
